Subject-level survival and segmentation evidence

survival-segmentation.Rmd

pytorch_aft and pytorch_discrete_hazard train baseline survival predictors under the existing node-enforced DP mechanism. The custodian must configure patient privacy and a stable subject identifier. Epsilon, delta, clipping, privacy-unit selection and the accounting population are not analyst controls. The original 28 contracts retain their API and registry records. Binary segmentation is included below with its public-initialisation evidence and separately labelled random-initialisation boundary comparisons.

Two subject likelihoods

The AFT contract uses a scalar location predictor mu(x) and a fixed public Weibull shape or log-normal sigma. dispersion is one of 0.5, 1, 2. The location is bounded to [-10,10], and incompatible public time/dispersion ranges fail before private data is accessed. Weibull uses its full event or censor likelihood; log-normal censor likelihood uses stable log_ndtr. Reported event density includes the original-time Jacobian.

model <- ds.flower.model.pytorch_aft(
  horizon = 1825, time_scale = 365,
  distribution = "lognormal", dispersion = 1,
  hidden_layers = integer(0))
fit <- ds.flower.fit(
  conns, symbol = "D", target = c("time", "event"),
  features = c("age", "baseline_covariate"), model = model,
  feature_bounds = list(lower = c(0, 0), upper = c(100, 1)),
  rounds = 10)

Time is measured in days from the declared baseline. Event coding is exactly 1=event, 0=right censoring. Finite times above the public horizon are administratively censored at the horizon; an event exactly at the horizon remains an event. Times below the public minimum resolution, nonfinite times, invalid event codes and duplicate subject records become safe placeholders with valid=0. They are never removed from the privacy census or denominator. No arithmetic averaging of survival outcomes occurs.

The hazard contract maps a covariate vector to K logits. K is at most 64. Intervals are (left, right]: an event contributes through its event interval; a censor contributes only completely observed intervals. Censoring inside an interval contributes no observed non-event for that incomplete interval.

model <- ds.flower.model.pytorch_discrete_hazard(
  edges = c(0, 7, 14, 21, 30, 45, 60, 90, 120,
            180, 270, 365, 540, 730, 1095, 1460, 1825))

For subject i, the loss is valid_i * sum(mask_ij * BCE(logit_ij,event_ij))/K. The batch loss is the mean over every sampled subject, including invalid subjects’ zero contributions. A tensor item contains the whole period vector; Opacus sums its period effects and clips that subject’s complete parameter gradient once. Periods are never flattened into independent training examples.

Censuses and privacy accounting

The source manifest retains M source rows and N subjects. A separate local, server-owned artifact holds N derived subject vectors. Both censuses and the exact source-to-subject transformation are checked before training. Invalid subjects do not reduce N. The accountant still uses q=1/ceiling(N/batch_size) and the complete pinned round/epoch horizon; K never multiplies N.

Replace-one conversion, secure Poisson draws, secure Gaussian noise, empty noisy steps and fixed client weights remain unchanged. Distribution, dispersion, interval edges, validity and effective transformed tensors are bound into sticky semantics. Repeating an equivalent release does not generate a new noise draw on the same deterministic software/device profile. Separate models, splits or experiments on overlapping real subjects compose.

Cox partial likelihood remains excluded because one subject’s risk set can change another subject’s gradient. Calling its event terms individual losses does not make them subject-separable.

Prediction and channel-B evaluation

Released artifacts retain the public model specification and survival settings. Local prediction reconstructs the same head and transformation:

risk <- ds.flower.predict(fit, public_test_features, type="risk")
curves <- ds.flower.predict(fit, public_test_features, type="survival",
                            times=c(30, 180, 365))
median <- ds.flower.predict(fit, public_test_features, type="median")

AFT risk is -mu; hazard risk is negative restricted mean survival over the public grid using left-endpoint survival. Hazard curves may cross. Curves are constant between hazard interval ends; a hazard median beyond the horizon is unavailable. AFT medians follow the selected public distribution.

Concordance and held-out NLL are evaluated only on public or independently authorized analyst-local data. The campaign excludes observed-time ties and awards half credit to exact risk ties. Its likelihood score uses original-time AFT density or hazard NLL divided by K. These are different likelihood scales; compare each contract with its own exact twin.

ds.flower.validate, private holdout, cross-validation and survival training inside HPO reject at public preflight. No private training losses, concordance, event counts or validity summaries are returned. This work does not implement competing risks, delayed entry, interval censoring or time-varying covariates.

Public evidence and preregistration

The protocol is distributed at tools/campaign/survival/PROTOCOL_F_SURVIVAL.md. It fixes subject splits before any scoring, a baseline-only covariate subset, public bounds, three seeds, three isolated DSLite sites, epsilon 1/4/8, delta 1e-5 and clip 1. SUPPORT2 is the primary cohort; LUNG1 is the small secondary cohort. Source hashes, split hashes, versions, exact commits, runner hashes and mechanism details accompany executed JSONs under inst/extdata/campaign/survival/.

SUPPORT2 (UCI 880) lists CC BY 4.0. The source description identifies day-3 assessments; this campaign excludes them and outcome-derived fields. TCIA LUNG1 clinical data is CC BY-NC 3.0 and measures survival from treatment start. The clinical file has noncommercial terms; it is not a commercial-use benchmark.

The preregistered primary floor is mean SUPPORT2 C-index at epsilon 8 at least 0.60 and at least null +0.05, assessed separately for each model. Failure is reported as failure. All four historical utility-envelope checks are empirical diagnostics, not privacy proofs. Here shortfall is G=central-federated, the reverse sign of the older article’s delta. Confidence intervals describe variation over matched public split replicates; overlapping splits and only three replicates limit their interpretation.

Log-normal AFT is the introductory example because the reviewer’s exploratory pooled probes found useful ranking and better held-out NLL than their covariate-free null. Those probes are not release evidence. Their Weibull arms (including nonprivate training) and hazard DP arms had worse NLL than their nulls under the fixed schedules. Concordance measures ranking, not probability calibration; inspect held-out NLL alongside concordance in the executed matrix. The current summary retains v1 AFT results and uses the selected h06 discrete-hazard schedule from the preregistered v2 confirmation: 10 rounds, 4 local epochs, batch size 64, learning rate 0.05, and 10 intervals. The selection record, preregistration, driver completion and all 30 confirmation cells are packaged under survival/hazard-v2/. The original v1 cells and survival/v1/summary.json remain boundary evidence. Schedule development and confirmation are distinguished in those records. The v2 confirmation reuses the public outer holdouts, so it is not independent external validation. LUNG1 v2 ran on pod CUDA whereas its v1 evidence used CPU; those schedules and device profiles must not be treated as a controlled schedule-only contrast. Failed utility floors remain reported, and reviewer promotion is separate from execution. For the executed matrix, lower NLL is better only relative to the matching null and likelihood family: a C-index floor or PASS does not establish calibrated probabilities. The rendered table therefore retains every exact twin’s NLL and labels whether federated-DP NLL is worse than its matched null.

Only archived executed cells support a measured-utility statement. A failed attempt has no substituted score. Promotion remains a reviewer decision after all mathematical, gradient, accounting, authority, staging, sticky and API compatibility gates pass.

Binary segmentation: current public initialisation and retained boundaries

The contract uses one selected image per subject, a frozen ImageNet ResNet-18 encoder, canonical 128 by 128 masks, and a subject-separable BCE/Dice loss. Invalid subjects remain in the privacy census with zero loss validity. Private validation, holdout, cross-validation and private-score HPO are unsupported. The binary segmentation guide describes the complete schema, prediction mapping and fail-closed boundaries.

Current results come from protocol v5, whose SHA256 begins 28a713f8. The selected public-initialisation route uses a narrow 9,521-parameter decoder, 60 public pretraining epochs on BUSI, 20 federated rounds and nominal batch 16. Batch 64 is a sensitivity arm. BUSI is the public dataset described by Al-Dhabyani et al. (2020), obtained through its Kaggle mirror; the packaged public-pretraining/audit.json, per-seed records and public-pretraining-manifest.json retain dataset, checkpoint and audit digests. The campaign’s audited benchmark binding loads public decoder tensors before private training. These results do not describe the default random decoder initialisation or a general analyst checkpoint-upload API.

The original packaged batch files were exact v3 copies. RECONCILE_V5.md and audit-results.json record the stale-file finding and fresh artifact-inference checks. Current batch16/ and batch64/ records now contain the actual v5 results; retained/v3/ and retained/v4/ retain random-initialisation boundary evidence. The comparison below labels each protocol explicitly and never pools their seeds. The v4-to-v5 comparison also changes decoder/schedule settings, so it does not isolate a causal effect of pretraining alone.
